activities.anchor: from a slogan into an electrical fact
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the heartbeat of multitasking
activities.name: osInterruptCloze

config.text: The %%0%% interrupt (typically %%1%%–1,000 times per second) hands the machine back to the supervisor no matter what a program is doing — the only reason one runaway program cannot own it. Software versions (%%2%%) are how system calls are implemented.
config.hint: The heartbeat of multitasking — and a page fault is one too, raised by the memory unit.

activities.caption: call the price of one miss
activities.name: osPagefaultEst

config.prompt: Fetching one missing chunk from disk costs roughly how many times a RAM access?
config.why: A fault lands in milliseconds against ~100 ns of RAM — which is why the swapping death spiral is the classic emergency.
config.context: L1 ≈ 1 ns, RAM ≈ 100 ns, SSD ≈ 100 µs (1,000× RAM), a spinning-disk seek ≈ 10 ms (100,000× RAM).

activities.anchor: Every subsequent program is a child of that chain
activities.caption: put the boot sequence in order
activities.name: osBootOrder

config.prompt: From power-on to your session — put the boot sequence in order:
items: The CPU executes firmware (UEFI), which initialises hardware and verifies the boot chain (secure boot checks signatures)
The bootloader (GRUB) loads the kernel image into memory and hands over control
The kernel mounts the root file system and starts init
init (systemd) spawns everything else: drivers, services, the login manager, your session
config.why: The boot log is a map of the whole architecture — and secure boot checks signatures along the way.

activities.anchor: Locality is the programmer's only lever
activities.caption: slide to the SSD's rung on the hierarchy
activities.name: osHierarchyPlace

config.prompt: The hierarchy in powers of nanoseconds: L1 at 10⁰, RAM at 10². Slide the marker to the SSD read.
config.why: SSD ≈ 100 µs = 10⁵ ns — 1,000× RAM; a spinning-disk seek ≈ 10 ms = 10⁷ ns. Touching nearby data together — array walks, not pointer chases — is worth 10–100× at zero cost.

activities.anchor: the scheduler's world is a small state machine
activities.caption: file each situation by what it does to the CPU
activities.name: osStatesSort

config.prompt: File each situation by what it does to the CPU:

items.label: blocked — waiting for disk, network or a lock

config.why: Blocked processes consume no time slices — which is why a thousand idle connections cost almost nothing.

activities.anchor: The kernel steers this machine with
activities.caption: pair each signal with its behaviour
activities.name: osSignalMatch

config.prompt: The software-interrupt zoo — pair each with its behaviour:

pairs.right: cannot be caught — the address space is simply reclaimed
the segment fault itself — delivered on touching an unmapped page
exited but whose status no one has collected — a parent's bookkeeping failure

config.why: Orphans get re-parented to init; fork clones the process and exec replaces it — understanding fork/exec is understanding the command line.

activities.anchor: The design trade has a name in every architecture
activities.caption: walk the concurrency-unit choice
activities.name: osUnitBranch

config.root: You are designing a web server. Walk the choice of concurrency unit.

start.text: One connection crashes with a pointer bug. What do you want to happen?

choices.label: Only that connection dies — isolation
choices.feedback: Process per connection — the historical fork model: heavy creation, cold caches, but the blast radius is one.

choices.label: Speed matters more — shared state, guarded
choices.feedback: Thread pools: cheap creation, warm caches, trivial communication — and every race, lock and deadlock hazard applies.

process.text: Isolation bought. What does a browser do about hostile sites?

choices.label: Sandbox each site in its own process
choices.feedback: Isolation bought back at process scale, with threads inside each sandbox for speed.

choices.label: One process for everything — simpler
choices.feedback: One stray site's pointer bug corrupts every open tab — the reason browsers pay the process price.

thread.text: Threads chosen. Guard the shared state.

choices.label: Locks around critical sections
choices.feedback: Indivisible critical sections cure races — and lock ordering is how you avoid the deadlock cycle.

chrome.text: The browser's model: process-per-site for isolation, threads inside for speed — the same dial at browser scale.

risk.text: A pointer bug in one thread corrupts a sibling rather than failing safely — isolation is why the browser pays for processes.

locks.text: Locks, atomics, and lock ordering to break the deadlock cycle — the discipline in your own server.

config.why: Threads exchange isolation for cheap communication; processes exchange communication cost for isolation — one dial, redrawn at all scales.

activities.caption: true or false — the kernel architecture argument
activities.name: osKernelJudge

statements.s: Monolithic kernels run everything in kernel mode for speed, at the price of a driver bug crashing the machine.
statements.why: Linux's model: fast, monolithic — one bad driver takes the whole system down.

statements.s: Microkernels keep a minimal core and push drivers to user-space servers for isolation.
statements.why: Minix, seL4, QNX — at a message-passing cost.

statements.s: seL4 is a monolithic kernel, formally proven fast.
statements.why: It is a verified MICROkernel — formally proven correct against its specification, the field's proof the dream is achievable.

statements.s: Containers share a kernel but isolate views; hypervisors give each guest OS the illusion of owning real hardware.
statements.why: Virtualisation is virtual memory's generalisation — the same trick, one level up.
